guide.p: Some words are not tied to one subject but appear again and again in academic texts of every kind — in science, economics, history and education. Knowing them well helps you read Academic passages faster and write Task 2 essays with a more formal, precise style.

bullets: Learn the word family: analyse (verb), analysis (noun), analytical (adjective).
Use them accurately in your own writing — a misused academic word costs more than a simple word used well.

guide.tip: When you meet one of these words in a Reading passage, underline it and note the word it collocates with (e.g. 'conduct research', 'significant increase').

vocab.meaning: to examine something in detail to understand it
vocab.example: Researchers analysed data from over 2,000 households.

vocab.meaning: a way of dealing with something
vocab.example: A more practical approach would be to tax fuel rather than ban cars.

vocab.meaning: to judge the quality, size or value of something
vocab.example: Teachers assess students' progress every term.

vocab.meaning: to believe something is true without proof
vocab.example: Many people assume that older workers are less productive.

vocab.meaning: an advantage; to gain an advantage (verb)
vocab.example: Small businesses benefit from lower taxes.

vocab.meaning: an idea or principle
vocab.example: The concept of a four-day working week is gaining popularity.

vocab.meaning: to be made of
vocab.example: The course consists of six modules and a final project.

vocab.meaning: the situation in which something happens
vocab.example: The figures only make sense in the context of rising prices.

vocab.meaning: to come from a particular source
vocab.example: Much of the town's income is derived from tourism.

vocab.meaning: to set up; or to discover a fact for certain
vocab.example: Scientists have established a link between sleep and memory.

vocab.meaning: to calculate roughly; a rough calculation
vocab.example: It is estimated that half of all food is wasted.

vocab.meaning: facts that show something is true (uncountable)
vocab.example: There is little evidence that the policy reduced crime.

vocab.meaning: one of several things that cause a result
vocab.example: Cost is a major factor in choosing a university.

vocab.meaning: the purpose of something; to work
vocab.example: The main function of a museum is to educate.

vocab.meaning: to recognise or find something
vocab.example: The report identifies three main causes of the problem.

vocab.meaning: to show or suggest
vocab.example: The results indicate that the treatment is effective.

vocab.meaning: to explain the meaning of something
vocab.example: The data can be interpreted in different ways.

vocab.meaning: to include as a necessary part (followed by -ing)
vocab.example: The job involves travelling abroad twice a month.

vocab.meaning: an important topic or problem
vocab.example: Housing is a major issue for young people.

vocab.meaning: a way of doing something
vocab.example: Online learning is now a common teaching method.

vocab.meaning: to happen (formal)
vocab.example: Most accidents occur within five kilometres of home.

vocab.meaning: a plan of action agreed by a government or organisation
vocab.example: The government introduced a new recycling policy.

vocab.meaning: a basic rule or belief
vocab.example: The scheme is based on the principle that polluters should pay.

vocab.meaning: to need (formal)
vocab.example: Most jobs now require basic computer skills.

vocab.meaning: large or important enough to notice
vocab.example: There was a significant rise in house prices.

vocab.meaning: where something comes from
vocab.example: Wind is an increasingly important source of energy.

vocab.meaning: to keep something going over time
vocab.example: The economy cannot sustain this rate of growth.

vocab.meaning: to be different in different situations
vocab.example: Rents vary widely from one city to another.
